title: Big Ten’s Tony Petitti takes different approach from SEC to ‘breakaway’ possibility
content:
CHICAGO — Big Ten commissioner Tony Petitti overwhelmingly embraced the on-field rivalry his conference has with the SEC, but he stopped short of committing toward breaking away from the NCAA should Congress fail to pass a Protect College Sports Act, unlike SEC counterpart Greg Sankey.

Petitti, who spoke for nearly 45 minutes Tuesday morning to open the three-day Big Ten media days event, instead focused on working with the SEC and other power conferences to provide a system more palatable to all entities, rather than striking out alone.

“Breakaway is … a word that creates a lot of emotion,” Petitti said. “I’ve never heard that anybody doesn’t want to play anybody else. We want to schedule more good games against teams that our fans expect. We’ve just got to get to a system that allows us to do that.

“I think every league is going to be in a position to say, what are we going to do that’s better than what we have now, and do we have to do it ourselves?”

At SEC media days last week in Tampa, Fla., Sankey said breakaway conversations are “real” and “I do not believe that is a leverage point.” Sankey reiterated later, like Petitti, that he prefers not to reach that point, but frustration over being unable to enforce the NCAA’s rules has bubbled over among SEC administrators. It’s similar for Big Ten brass, but the rhetoric is more measured publicly.

On major issues, Petitti said the commissioners operate in lockstep, especially when it comes to the Senate bill that could reshape the makeup of college sports. However, the two commissioners remain apart when it comes to Petitti’s plan for a 24-team College Football Playoff. Sankey prefers a 16-team postseason tournament or, at a minimum, wants more information related to revenues on eliminating conference championships to accommodate a larger CFP. Those answers should come in mid-August.

“Working with the SEC on the Playoff and working with Greg specifically, I’ve never heard him say that he won’t do the work and consider 24,” Petitti said. “He’s been public about certain preferences he has, but he’s committed himself to doing the work around all formats, and we’ve done the same thing. We have strong opinions about where the right path is.

“I think there’s been an evolution since we were here last year about how people feel about 24 at this point, and we’ve made adjustments in our league. We were focused on automatic qualifiers (in 2025). We’re not focused on that anymore.”

The Big Ten and SEC are college sports’ highest-profile leagues with each earning more than $1 billion in revenue during fiscal 2025. The Big Ten has won the past three CFP championships and owns an 8-2 postseason record against the SEC in the last two postseasons. The SEC, however, largely owned the sport before the 12-team CFP, which was implemented in 2024.

Officials and coaches from both conferences often tout their collective strength and depth. League and school officials from both leagues have met twice in person and expressed interest in playing one another more frequently in the regularly season, which Petitti said “let’s just keep doing that.”

In the 2024-25 CFP semifinals, Ohio State outlasted Texas en route to the CFP championship. Last fall, the top-ranked Longhorns opened the season at No. 2 Ohio State, a game the Buckeyes won 14-7. This year, Ohio State travels to Austin, Texas. In addition, Oklahoma travels to Michigan and Mississippi State heads to Minnesota. Originally, Nebraska was set to face Tennessee, but the Cornhuskers dropped the series in order to schedule another home game.

“Our fans, I think the SEC fans, they really like the rivalry,” Petitti said. “I think it would be great if we played each other more. I think that’s from a fan perspective. Having a rivalry with the Big Ten, the SEC, is a great pair. You see the games when we play them in the CFP, we play them in the regular season, which isn’t that often right now.

“Fans really want to compete. They want to talk about which league is better.”
